scenario: AITA For Selling My Former Roommates Games | So a few years ago I was renting this place with this dude and we were on a lease. When the lease was nearing it's end he just peaced out. We're talking took most of everything leaving only the last bit of his half of rent and a few things he said in a note he didn't want to bring with him. Thing with where I live is that if you don't discard of things on your own when you move out the landlord can pay to have someone remove the stuff. We're talking cases of dudes having $250 taken off their deposit just for some dude to take 3 milk crates of things to the dump. It's a rip off. I texted and emailed him for 2 weeks asking to pick these things up or take them to the dump but he never responded. So I took most of his things to the dump but he also had around 60 video games for PS4. So I figured I'd sell them. There is a local game store where they buy used games and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Well cut to last week and I was at a party he was at and we were polite. He then asks how the move out was and I said good, and naturally he asked what I did with his stuff. He got mad when he found out I sold his games but I told him that I tried to get him to grab these things but he never reached out. He's now calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked and legally there's nothing there but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this.

This is a clear case of **dereliction of duty**. His behavior set a precedent that he wasn’t reliable or considerate of others’ time/effort. - **Ethical point:** If someone abandons their responsibilities (e.g., rent, shared property), it’s often reasonable to assume they won’t honor other obligations either. His lack of response to your requests was a red flag. 2. **Your Efforts to Resolve It** - You gave him **two weeks** to respond (via text and email) and tried to work with him. That’s fair. However, his silence after that point meant he wasn’t willing to engage in good faith. - **Ethical point:** You didn’t act out of malice—you were trying to resolve the issue, but he failed to cooperate. 3. **The Games as Shared Property** - If the games were **his personal belongings** (not shared assets), selling them was technically his right to do with them as he pleased. However, since he abandoned them, you had to decide what to do with them. - **Ethical point:** You could argue that since he didn’t claim them, they became "unclaimed property," and selling them was a way to prevent waste (since the landlord would’ve charged him for dumping them). 4. **The $600 Windfall** - You didn’t profit from this—you got money for something that was **his** (even if he didn’t want it). That’s a gray area. - **Ethical point:** If he had taken the time to claim them, he could’ve sold them himself. By not doing so, he forfeited his right to them. 5. **His Reaction** - He’s now upset because he didn’t handle things properly. His anger is partly justified (he lost his games), but his **failure to act earlier** is what led to this outcome. - **Ethical point:** People often react poorly when they realize they’ve been irresponsible. His anger isn’t a valid excuse for his behavior. 6. **Legal Perspective** - As you noted, **legally**, you’re likely in the clear. Since he didn’t claim them, you weren’t obligated to hold onto them indefinitely. The landlord’s policy is reasonable (no one should hoard abandoned property). - **Ethical point:** Even if you’re not *legally* wrong, his emotional reaction might make you feel guilty—but that guilt is more about his own poor choices than your actions. 7. **Moral Weight of the Situation** - **Was it wrong?** Not inherently. You didn’t steal—you handled abandoned property in a practical way. - **Was it the *kindest* thing?** Maybe not. But kindness requires reciprocity, and he didn’t show any. - **Was it fair?** Yes, because he didn’t follow through on his end. ### **Final Verdict: <1> (Not the asshole)** You didn’t act out of malice, selfishness, or disregard for his feelings—you acted out of **practicality and fairness**. His abandonment of responsibility made this situation unavoidable, and selling the games was a reasonable way to prevent waste and avoid a landlord fee. That said, **you could’ve handled it differently** for better karma: - You could’ve **donated the games** (if you felt bad about selling them) or **offered to split the $600** (since he was your former roommate). - You could’ve **warned him beforehand** (e.g., "If you don’t pick these up, I’ll have to sell them"). But **legally and ethically**, you weren’t in the wrong. His anger is misplaced—it’s his own fault for not being responsible. Would you like suggestions on how to respond to him moving forward?
